content: The systematic collection and analysis of data, disaggregated by sex, age, and other factors, is essential to better understand the health-seeking behaviors of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases and their caregivers. This approach is critical for identifying gender-related barriers to health-seeking behavior. The findings from such analyses should be utilized to implement effective and timely modifications in AFP surveillance activities, particularly those aimed at enhancing active surveillance, case detection, and the transportation of specimens. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) strategy has established a targeted timeline for case investigations, while the Global Polio Surveillance Action Plan (GPSAP) 2022–2024 specifies a 35-day window from the onset of disease to the final laboratory result. Annex 4 outlines various types of delays in detection, their potential causes, and strategies for addressing them within the program. AFP surveillance should undergo regular national reviews to evaluate its effectiveness. Integration of AFP surveillance with other vaccine-preventable diseases (VPD) surveillance, including data triangulation (e.g., comparisons of coverage, surveillance, and other data sources), is recommended. During quarterly Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) data review meetings, the coverage and performance of the surveillance program should be assessed at both national and subnational levels to identify gaps or areas requiring strengthened surveillance. A comprehensive national review of surveillance, including field components, should be conducted every five years. In larger countries, provincial reviews should be carried out annually, ensuring all provinces are covered within a five-year cycle. All instances of wild poliovirus (WPV), vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV), and Sabin-like type 2 viruses must be reported immediately by national authorities to the World Health Organization (WHO), regardless of the isolate type or source (clinical case, environmental sample, or other). The detection of WPV in any area must prompt an appropriate and timely response, including rapid and thorough epidemiological investigation, strengthening of AFP surveillance in the affected area, and immediate implementation of appropriate immunization activities. Environmental surveillance (ES) has been established in six countries in the WHO South-East Asia Region as of 2022: Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Nepal, and Thailand. While AFP surveillance remains the gold standard for poliovirus detection, ES can be more effective in certain settings, such as areas with suboptimal AFP surveillance or populations with high vaccination coverage or those receiving inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). Countries can use a combination of ES and AFP surveillance to maintain high sensitivity and specificity levels. ES has been instrumental in detecting and monitoring the reintroduction of WPV into polio-free countries and in providing confidence in the successful elimination of the virus in areas with prior transmission. In polio-free countries, ES can supplement AFP surveillance to detect WPV reintroduction or circulating VDPV (cVDPV) emergence, document poliovirus release from vaccine manufacturing facilities or laboratories, and monitor the disappearance of Sabin strains following the withdrawal of oral polio vaccine (OPV). In countries with recent polio events or outbreaks, ES can document the scope of virus transmission, guide immunization activities, assess the effectiveness of vaccination campaigns, and confirm the end of an outbreak by demonstrating the absence of VDPV or WPV in the environment alongside negative stool samples from AFP cases. The success of ES requires collaboration among epidemiologists, local public health officials, WHO staff, sanitary engineering authorities, and technical staff involved in wastewater and sewage infrastructure maintenance, as well as staff from the Global Polio Laboratory Network (GPLN) responsible for processing samples. When selecting ES sampling sites, it is important to target high-risk populations, typically within a catchment size of 100,000 to 300,000 individuals. Urban areas, transit hubs, and other high-priority locations should be evaluated for feasibility. Sampling sites should be sensitive, with enteroviruses detected in at least 50% of samples. The type of sewer system (e.g., closed networks, open canals, or water channels) and the presence of toxic compounds that may interfere with poliovirus detection must also be considered. Accessibility to sampling sites, particularly during early morning hours when toilet use peaks, is critical. Sites in areas with dangerous terrain, active conflict, or life-threatening violence should be avoided. Sampling schedules should optimize transportation and laboratory resources, with routine or permanent sites sampled at least once a month. Temporary sites, established during outbreaks, should operate for no less than 12 months with intensified AFP surveillance. Sampling frequency and site locations can be adjusted as needed in consultation with public health agencies and the GPEI. New environmental sites should undergo a validation period of 6–12 months, during which performance is analyzed before formal inclusion in the surveillance network. Decisions to close sampling sites should involve thorough investigations and discussions with the WHO regional office. Reasons for closure may include underperformance, changes in program needs, or limitations in ES processing capacity. The decision-making process must be systematic, with documentation shared with the WHO regional office and, if necessary, WHO headquarters.
